ety.text: From Middle English *bussen (suggested by Middle English bussyng (“buzzing”)), of onomatopoeic origin. Cognate with Scots bizz (“to buzz”). Compare Middle English bunning (“buzzing”), Middle English hossing (“buzzing”), Middle English bissen (“to hush”).

senses.d: A continuous humming noise, as of bees; a confused murmur, as of general conversation in low tones.
ex: In the steady buzz of flies the homeward-bound agent was lying flushed and insensible[.]

senses.d: The audible friction of voiced consonants.
A rush or feeling of energy or excitement; a feeling of slight intoxication.
ex: Still feeling the buzz from the coffee, he pushed through the last of the homework.
Now, don't waste time, give us a buzz -- quick! 825-4703 or 265-7881.

senses.d: Major topic of conversation; widespread rumor; information spread behind the scenes.
ex: Mr. Hall? The buzz on Christian is that his parents have joint custody, so he'll be spending one semester in Chicago and one semester here.
In Detroit, the buzz is that he's too nice a guy, unwilling to impose draconian job cuts at the risk of angering the UAW.

senses.d: To make a low, continuous, humming or sibilant sound, like that made by bees with their wings.
ex: Ah! the singing, fatal arrow, / Like a wasp it buzzed, and stung him [a roebuck]!

senses.d: To utter a murmuring sound; to speak with a low, humming voice.
ex: However these disturbers of our peace / Buzz in the people's ears.

senses.d: Of a group of people, to talk about some interesting topic excitedly.
To fly while making such a sound.
ex: A fly was buzzing past me.
The flies, lethargic with the autumn, were beginning to buzz into the room.

senses.d: To show a high level of activity and haste, energization or excitement, to be busy as a bee in one’s actions but perhaps mentally charged.
ex: The room was buzzing with excitement.

senses.d: To whisper; to communicate, as tales, in an undertone; to spread, as a report, by whispers or secretly.
ex: I will buzz abroad such prophecies / That Edward shall be fearful of his life.

senses.d: To talk to incessantly or confidentially in a low humming voice.
To fly at high speed and at a very low altitude over (an area), as to make a surprise pass.
ex: buzzing around in small cars that dodged through traffic

senses.d: To cut (the hair) in a close-cropped military style, or buzzcut.

ex: I have mentioned her deft hand with a stone — well, as soon as our backs were turned she buzzed a stone to clip Joe's ear.

ety.text: Onomatopoeic. Possibly from Middle High German brūsen + -io (frequentative), from Old High German *brūsen, from Proto-Germanic *brausijaną (“to break; crack; crackle”).

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Latin -itusder. Spanish -ido Spanish zumbido From zumbar + -ido.

Borrowed from Late Latin enthūsiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós, “inspiration, enthusiasm”), from ἔνθεος (éntheos, “possessed by a god”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θεός (theós, “god”).

senses.d: The sound produced by something that buzzes.
ex: I can hear buzzing coming from the television.

senses.d: Very happy; full of joyful excitement.
ex: 'She was buzzing, mate, I tell you. She was so funny to listen to. It's the happiest phone call I've had off her in a while.'

grp.label: sound produced by something that buzzes
